CARTE BLANCHE FLIES TO THE DRC

By: Michael Duffett | Delivery

Proposal


Show:

Summary:
Carte Blanche flies to the DRC, to see how our soldiers contribute to the massive peace-keeping mission in one of Africa’s most volatile countries. As the only UN mission with a mandate to use lethal force, our troops are often called upon to engage a range of rebel groups based in dense forests and isolated bases. Our interviewees will include courageous Rooivalk helicopter pilots who routinely fly over rebel-held territory to while providing aerial support to ground forces. We’ll also speak to General Derek Mgwebi, the South African general recently appointed as head of the overall UN mission in the DRC. Our SANDF fixer will endeavor to ensure we are given access to the frontlines, and arrange helicopter transport to the areas in which the SANDF troops operate.

Press Release:


Exclusive: SANDF in the DRC
Escorted by the legendary Rooivalk combat helicopter, Carte Blanche travels to a recently-captured military camp deep in the tropical forests north of Beni, in the Democratic Republic of Congo. John Webb gains exclusive access to the SANDF’s forward-operating bases in the infamous Triangle of Death in North Kivu province as we visit our soldiers on the frontline in the battle against ADF rebels. We find soldiers who have distinguished themselves both in the field of battle as well as in crucial combat support roles, and SANDF pilots operating as part of the UN's aviation unit who have fast developed a reputation for skill and courage. Carte Blanche also meets the SANDF's General Derrick Mgwebi who was recently appointed to head the overall UN peace-keeping operation in the DRC - still the largest peace-keeping mission in the world.


Script:


Ever since the overthrow of the dictator mabutu seseko 1997, what is now known as the democratic republic Congo, has lurched from one crisis to the next. A shaky peace deal that brought a halt to a bloody civil war in 1999 which had claimed the lives of millions of people, allowed for the intervention of the United Nations. It established a mission then known as Monarch, which remains the largest peace keeping operation in the world – around 20 thousand personnel, and is still in place in the DRC 17 years later.

We travelled to the capital, Kinshasa, to meet South African General, Derrick Mgwebi, who, in a significant show of faith by the UN, has been appointed as the officer commanding the entire mission in the DRC. Now called Monusco it includes about 14 00 South African Defense Force members contributing to the mission as part of our foreign policy commitments. – Providing aerial support for troops, an engineering core for infrastructure and supporting the Congolese army in fighting the rebels.

The general has a significant task on his hands with at least nine different rebel groups fighting against the Congolese army and amongst themselves.

John: Were you ever daunted by the challenge? It's such a complex issue; do you ever find it overwhelming?
Mgwebi: Of course it is quite a challenge. The size of the country itself where you can put the better half of western Europe and also if you look at the history of the country in terms of the conflict which they find themselves in. The complexity of the situation makes it quite a daunting task.

One of the units under his overall command in headquarters at this command in Kinshasa. This unit is responsible for coordinating the massive logistical operation to support the entire mission in the DRC - that includes fixing vehicles, loading cargoes into planes, arranging transport to and from home for the troops. Because the military isn’t subject to a civilian police force, one of its biggest responsibilities is organizing an efficient military police presence. One member on the base feels that his position is the most important, and that’s the postmaster.

Danie Oosthuysen: Actually this job is very important cause it works on a person’s morale. Mail boosts your morale. You can go without food but you need your parcel or your letters to boost your morale.

Since the start to the UN mission Kinshasa has been relatively peaceful. It’s the east of the country that remains most volatile, with several active rebel groups. So in the early hours of the morning we headed to city’s airport to catch a UN charted flight.

LINK: Over the years the mission in Kinshasa has been scaled down substantially with more efforts focused on Goma which is called the operational area and that is where we are heading now.

The trip east took two hours and because we were travelling with general mbanga, on landing we were met with a guard of honor.

JOHN: Just across the waters of Lake Kivu lies Rwanda. Now in order to understand what in part led to the instability in the DRC, you need to understand what happened over there in 1994.

That’s when during a 3 months period which will be remembered as one of the darkest chapters in Africa’s history. Close to a million people were mascaraed in the Rwandan genocide the slaughter triggered a civil war, which led to hundreds of thousands of people feeling into the neighboring DRC. Amongst them them were many of the perpetrators of the genocide where they have maintained a presence to this day. To fund their operations, they and other more recent rebel groups exploit the area vast mineral wealth.

LINK: This is Goma; it’s the main headquarters of MONUSCO in eastern DRC. Back in 2013 it was overrun by a rebel group calling itself M23.

Their march into goma was met with little resistance. But if the rebels thought that they could control the city with impunity, they were mistaken. For the first time ever the un set up a force to target and neutralize the rebels armies in the eastern DRC. M23 was first in their sights. The so-called force intervention brigade consisting of solders from South Africa, Malawi and Tanzania launched an offensive against the rebels that not only drove them out goma but also led to their eventual surrender.

LINK: Driving around Goma, it’s hard to imagine that at one time not that long ago this was effectively the front line. But driving with an escort like this one is a reminder that at times things can still be a little tense.

The headquarters of monusco's air wing in this region is at goma airport where the combat Helicopter Unit is stationed.

Heading up the SA base is helicopter pilot colonel abel naik.

John: Big responsibility. I guess a lot of that is on your shoulders?
Colonel Naik: Yes it is a big responsibility because having aircraft in the mission area, it’s vital to the operation. I know it is always said that the air force doesn’t win wars because it’s by the boots on the ground but we bring them quite close to winning the war.

Under his command are 18 South African pilot, flight engineers and navigators. One combat helicopter stands out amongst all others at the base.

LINK: The victory against the M23 rebels would almost certainly not have been as decisive was it not for one particular piece of south African military hardware, the now legendary rooivalk combat support helicopter.

Its known for its ability to provide extremely accurate air support for troops on the ground - we met with two crewmembers. Weather conditions remain their biggest challenge.

Major Ramoipone: You can leave here when you come back its pouring like nobody's business, especially in the rainy season so its a very challenging.

And confidence in each other’s abilities is paramount.

Colonel Smit: So trust is vital. So he needs to have trust in me making the correct decisions, ensuring that we not firing on our own forces for instance and I need to trust him handling the aircraft.

The workforce of the air wing is the Oryx helicopter. It's known for its ability to land where no other troop-carrying helicopter dares to. Besides carrying troops to and from conflict areas, it also picks up rebels who have surrendered and it performs medical evacuations. One of its pilots is Major Charles Tarentaal whose child hood dreams became a reality.

Major Tarentaal: 30 years to the dream to the reality and its really not a moment regretted. Some say its madness but unless you here, you not going to understand it so yes 30 years and this is what we doing. So we really really loving it.

Often forgotten are the people are those who keep these aircraft serviced and able to fly at a moment’s notice.

John: So sergeant when you talk to people around the base, they say that the guys with the most important job are you guys. Is that true?
Sgt. Moshidi: I would say partly true but from what I have heard when we are not around it tends to get tense outside. So yes you can say that we are the most important guys.

And looking after the security at the base and responsible for the armed escorts is Sgt Maggie Rasesemola.

John: IT remains a bit of a touchy subject but how have the men under your leadership responded to you?
Sgt. Rasesemola: They have responded pretty well. I think everybody has adapted to the fact that we've moved on as a country where as you have woman in leadership and I haven’t had any problems whatsoever.

Morale at the base appears upbeat and which is perhaps attributed to the leadership style of Colonel Naik.

Col. Naik: Discipline remains number 1 priority. The members on the unit when I arrived here. Morale was already at a high. Now it is coming closer to the end of their deployment, it’s starting to drop a bit but like I said, I give them their space. I give them their time to de-stress because I believe I get more out of them after they get a chance to relax


And a high morale is crucial especially as the mission has now entered another phase. The force intervention brigade has opened up a new front against a group of notorious Islamic rebels, the ADF, with a reputation of being determined fighters.

John: so are these battles constant? Are we almost always engaging the rebels?
Mgwebi: Well it’s almost an everyday occurrence.

And notably in dense and hostile forest.

Mgwebi: To get to where they are, to travel 3km is almost 3 days work.

Colonel Dyakopu is second in charge of the force intervention brigade and has grown familiar with their modus operands.

Gen. Dyakopu: With the M23 it was a group of soldiers that took over Goma by force coming as waves whereas with the ADF you are dealing with counter insurgence.

And the dense forest is key to their operations.

Gen. Dyakopu: The forest is a good cover for them so if they lose the triangle then there is little space for them to survive.

The colonel is referring to the infamous triangle of death, an area of jungle, which the ADF are able to conceal them in. It’s in the far northern parts of north Kivu province.

LINK: While the headquarters of the operational area is here in Goma, the frontline is about an hour’s flight north of here and that is where we are heading now.

This would be the first time a news crew has been allowed into the operational area by the SANDF and UN. Our first stop was a staging point at an airfield just outside the triangle. As we landed we were greeted by the welcome sight of two rooivalk heliports. They had been conducting operations in the area and would be escorting us to the front. In the hour that followed we were given a situational report by colonel mbawsi. We were told that the area was volatile and that in the previous week helicopters had been fired upon. The triangle was worthy of its reputation.

LINK: So we have been told that we have to wear flat jackets and helmets for the trip to the perimeter bases and that’s because the last attack took place about a week ago so it is what you might call a little hostile.

In the preceding months the force intervention brigade had steadily driven the ADF rebels further north. As they advanced they took control and occupied several rebel camps and it was to one of these we headed. This was the front line.

We landed on territory captured from the ADF two months ago in a fierce battle.

LINK: This is camp abiolose surrounded by almost impenetrable jungle. It is the frontline against the ADF. A lookout point just across the valley from here was last attacked just 5 days ago.

The reason for that attack was that the ADF had lost their position, this hill known as camp garlic two weeks previously. They clearly wanted it back. But for know it remains secure and occupied by a contingent of Congolese soldiers.

Photographs taken of the camp show bunkers and tunnels used by rebels for fortification. And in the thick of the battle for Camp Garlic was none other than General Mgwebi.

Mgwebi: There is a need to go out because the understanding of the situation at that level is critical to be able to make the strategies to fight and prosecute the war we are faced with.

LINK: One of the hallmarks of the ADF is to attack the civilian population living in the dense forested area in the triangle as this is known. Some of the atrocities that they have committed against the local population are quite staggering.

And scenes like this are always difficult for our troops to witness

Captain Titus: Well its not an easy sight to see people being maimed, heads chopped off, maimed with machetes. Sometimes you find children and woman also beaten axed and stabbed with knives, brutally murdered. The smell of death and also to look at it sometimes, it affects you psychologically.


With the rooivalk sweeping overhead, anxious to escort us out of the operational area, we were able to catch up with men and women of Bravo Company of the 4th South African infantry battalion. And whose responsibility it is to hold onto this position against the ADF. They and the Congolese army who occupy the other side of the hill live in difficult conditions surviving on ration packs, a limited supply of water and constantly fighting off insects. But there was one complaint, which was common amongst all of them.

Sound up: Very hot...

We were then extracted off the hill accompanied by an impressive escort and headed back to goma. The journey back provided time for reflection not only on the contribution of the sandf to the UN mission but also on the extraordinary potential of this vast and beautiful country.

LINK: We came to the DRC unsure of what we would find. There is a perception back in SA that finding shortfalls have limited the effectiveness of the SANDF but as far as this mission is concerned, this is a story of South African excellence.

But the DRC is once again on a knifes edge. Elections are scheduled for November has been delayed and there are fears of more intense fighting as a result. So that excellence might soon be tested.

This would be the first time a news crew has been allowed into the operational area by the SANDF and UN. Our first stop was a staging point at an airfield just outside the triangle. As we landed we were greeted by the welcome sight of two rooivalk heliports. They had been conducting operations in the area and would be escorting us to the front. In the hour that followed we were given a situational report by colonel mbawsi. We were told that the area was volatile and that in the previous week helicopters had been fired upon. The triangle was worthy of its reputation. LINK: So we have been told that we have to wear flat jackets and helmets for the trip to the perimeter bases and that’s because the last attack took place about a week ago so it is what you might call a little hostile. In the preceding months the force intervention brigade had steadily driven the ADF rebels further north. As they advanced they took control and occupied several rebel camps and it was to one of these we headed. This was the front line. We landed on territory captured from the ADF two months ago in a fierce battle. LINK: This is camp abiolose surrounded by almost impenetrable jungle. It is the frontline against the ADF. A lookout point just across the valley from here was last attacked just 5 days ago. The reason for that attack was that the ADF had lost their position, this hill known as camp garlic two weeks previously. They clearly wanted it back. But for know it remains secure and occupied by a contingent of Congolese soldiers. Photographs taken of the camp show bunkers and tunnels used by rebels for fortification. And in the thick of the battle for Camp Garlic was none other than General Mgwebi. Mgwebi: There is a need to go out because the understanding of the situation at that level is critical to be able to make the strategies to fight and prosecute the war we are faced with. LINK: One of the hallmarks of the ADF is to attack the civilian population living in the dense forested area in the triangle as this is known. Some of the atrocities that they have committed against the local population are quite staggering. And scenes like this are always difficult for our troops to witness Captain Titus: Well its not an easy sight to see people being maimed, heads chopped off, maimed with machetes. Sometimes you find children and woman also beaten axed and stabbed with knives, brutally murdered. The smell of death and also to look at it sometimes, it affects you psychologically. With the rooivalk sweeping overhead, anxious to escort us out of the operational area, we were able to catch up with men and women of Bravo Company of the 4th South African infantry battalion. And whose responsibility it is to hold onto this position against the ADF. They and the Congolese army who occupy the other side of the hill live in difficult conditions surviving on ration packs, a limited supply of water and constantly fighting off insects. But there was one complaint, which was common amongst all of them. Sound up: Very hot... We were then extracted off the hill accompanied by an impressive escort and headed back to goma. The journey back provided time for reflection not only on the contribution of the sandf to the UN mission but also on the extraordinary potential of this vast and beautiful country. LINK: We came to the DRC unsure of what we would find. There is a perception back in SA that finding shortfalls have limited the effectiveness of the SANDF but as far as this mission is concerned, this is a story of South African excellence. But the DRC is once again on a knifes edge. Elections are scheduled for November has been delayed and there are fears of more intense fighting as a result. So that excellence might soon be tested. metadata.Summary: Carte Blanche flies to the DRC, to see how our soldiers contribute to the massive peace-keeping mission in one of Africa’s most volatile countries. As the only UN mission with a mandate to use lethal force, our troops are often called upon to engage a range of rebel groups based in dense forests and isolated bases. Our interviewees will include courageous Rooivalk helicopter pilots who routinely fly over rebel-held territory to while providing aerial support to ground forces. We’ll also speak to General Derek Mgwebi, the South African general recently appointed as head of the overall UN mission in the DRC. Our SANDF fixer will endeavor to ensure we are given access to the frontlines, and arrange helicopter transport to the areas in which the SANDF troops operate.
